title: Lesson 19: Security Ownership: Threat Model for Your AI Stack
description: Grounded in Lesson 19 of the AI Adoption series: what a threat model is and why AI breaks the security assumptions behind it, the five-step method for building one (assets, data classification, threats, scoring, named ownership), and the rule that security is a set of named jobs with one accountable owner per risk rather than shared responsibility.

questions.question: Lesson 19 argues that a threat model is the right tool for governing AI security because it moves the hard decisions out of the incident. What does a completed threat model exist to force?
options: To eliminate every risk so no incident can ever occur
To make sure every material risk has a named person accountable for it and a concrete action you can verify, decided before an incident assigns the accountability for you
To replace the organization's security team so no extra review is needed
To prove the AI tool is safe enough that the vendor's contract covers all responsibility
questions.explanation: Lesson 19 states the purpose plainly: the point is to force accountability so the question 'who owns this?' has a named answer before an incident answers it. A threat list only works if the accountability is real, and the step that makes it real is naming an owner and a concrete action for every risk above low. The lesson does not claim to eliminate risk, which it calls impossible.

questions.question: In the lesson's method, data classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted) matters because it does what for governing AI use?
options: It allows a blanket rule that bans all AI tools, which solves the security problem by removing the exposure

It lets you set a clear line: public and scrubbed internal data may enter a public tool, while confidential and restricted data gets a named rule about whether it can enter a tool at all, rather than a vague 'be careful'
It is only needed by regulated industries and can be skipped by every other organization
It is used to score likelihood, not to decide what may enter a tool
questions.explanation: Lesson 19 explains that the tension between locking everything down and letting everything expose you is resolved with classification, not a blanket rule. Classifying data lets you say a clean sentence people can follow, about what may go into a tool and under what conditions, instead of a vague warning. Restricted data, like client account numbers, is the kind that should never cross a boundary it should not cross.

questions.question: Lesson 19 warns against spreading responsibility across security, IT, legal, and the business team until everyone is 'loosely responsible.' What does the governance practice the lesson cites argue instead?
options: That a committee of all those teams should approve every low-risk internal tool

That shared input is useful but is not shared accountability, so each AI use case needs one named accountable owner, with an independent challenge that reviews the risk rather than relying on the person who is most excited about the tool
That the CISO should personally own every technology, legal, employee, and business consequence of AI
That the vendor's contract should be treated as the accountable owner since it names the liabilities
questions.explanation: Lesson 19 quotes the AI risk governance practice: shared input is not shared accountability, and when accountability is split, difficult decisions tend to wait. So each use case gets one named accountable owner, and the person promoting the use case should not be the only one deciding its risk is acceptable, which is why an independent challenge or governance committee reviews the decision. The vendor contract is explicitly called 'a piece of paper,' not an owner.
